evidence: Hor. C. 4.11.9–10: hūc et illūc cursitant
terms.comment: To a place away from both of us; hūc et illūc, this way and that.

evidence: Cato Agr. 1.2: utī eō introeās et circumspiciās
Caes. BG 1.25.5: eō sē recipere coepērunt
terms.comment: The unemphatic “(to) there”; it answers quō. Not the verb eō, I go.

phrases.latin: utī eō introeās et circumspiciās, utī inde exīre possīs
phrases.english: go in there and look round, so that you can get out of there again

phrases.latin: circumsiliēns modo hūc modo illūc ad sōlam dominam ūsque pīpiābat
phrases.english: hopping about, now this way, now that, it kept cheeping to its mistress alone

phrases.latin: Concēde istūc paululum: audīn'? etiam nunc paululum: sat est.
phrases.english: Move over there a little — do you hear? — a little more — that’s enough.

phrases.latin: Quō tē agis? — Egone? in aedem Veneris. — Quid eō?
phrases.english: Where are you off to? — Me? To the temple of Venus. — What are you going there for?

phrases.latin: cūncta festīnat manus, hūc et illūc cursitant mixtae puerīs puellae
phrases.english: the whole household bustles; girls and boys together run this way and that

sources: Lewis & Short: illuc · Lewis & Short: eo · Lewis & Short: istuc
